added_claims.speaker: Yav Git
added_claims.quote: the way you do the risk anal the risk control on it the way you manage the position um actually needs to be different because it
added_claims.claim: Crypto has enormous right skew, so risk control and position management for trend in crypto should differ from other asset classes; a generalist implementation leaves alpha on the table.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare skew-aware vs standard vol sizing on crypto trend

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: you wouldn't have the same person executing cash equities as you would have executing cash Bonds in a CT anyway
added_claims.claim: Rob rejects Yav's case for single-asset-class funds: specialised execution already exists inside a multi-asset CTA, and a generalised optimiser and risk model can handle differing diversification and distributions; he also calls Yav's sustained-imbalance theory of trends unproven.
added_claims.testable: partly - compare generalised vs asset-class-specific implementations

added_claims.speaker: Graham Robertson
added_claims.quote: liquidity is a term that's often misused you can talk about the size of the market and people will call that liquidity of the market but it's not necessarily the same thing
added_claims.claim: Market size is not liquidity: the industry players who dominate a market and its transaction costs shape how it trades and how trend performs there, so a single 'how liquid' measure is misleading.
added_claims.indicator: market size vs transaction costs vs participant mix

added_claims.speaker: Graham Robertson
added_claims.quote: larger investors tend to have an allocation to Trend following thick and thin
added_claims.claim: Large institutions keep a steady trend-following allocation through good and bad years, but wealth-segment investors and the media largely ignore it (an FT article on handling volatility did not mention trend following), which is where under-allocation lies.

added_claims.speaker: Yav Git
added_claims.quote: do you pay performance fee to your execution desk
added_claims.claim: Due-diligence test: asking whether a CTA pays its execution desk a performance fee reveals whether it treats execution as an alpha source or as a production line.

added_claims.speaker: Yav Git
added_claims.quote: the benefits of waiting far outweighs the loss of alpha even for those markets
added_claims.claim: Yav claims patient execution saves more than the alpha lost from delay even in liquid bond futures (e.g. 5-year Bobl), not only in illiquid OTC bonds; Rob disagrees for liquid futures.
added_claims.indicator: execution cost vs signal-delay alpha decay
added_claims.testable: yes - compare spread savings from passive fills vs alpha decay from delay

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the host (Niels) says 'let me just ask one thing Rob and then I'll let you jump in' and challenges Yav from his CTA vantage point. The dating of the end of the secular rate decline (around 2010) is Yav's reply, not part of this argument.
corrections.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: fixed income dominates CTA P&L because it is the largest, most liquid sector and enjoyed a 30-40 year favourable trend; it has made little recently, so focusing on it risks fitting to the past.

corrections.issue: Speaker: Yav Git says this, summarising Rob's blog, and adds his own objection; Rob does not speak here.
corrections.fix: Yav Git: Rob's blog found no correlation between market liquidity and trend performance; Yav agrees but argues the wrong liquidity is measured (the imbalance matters), and liquidity mainly limits diversification and capacity.

corrections.issue: Probable wrong speaker: the high-vol share class remark ('I remember back in the day and I'm sure it's still the case AHL was offering High Vol share classes') is by a former AHL person and continues into Rob's 'I like Yav saying...'; it is most likely Rob Carver, not Graham (current AHL CEO).
corrections.fix: Rob Carver (probable): high-vol share classes give capital efficiency, but few allocators see high vol as good and many prefer low-vol funds; changing the products may be the lever.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: Niels says this ('that's just my own view here') and moves to the next topic in the same turn.
corrections.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: heavy government bond issuance to fund policy changes means trend following should also be considered as protection for fixed-income portfolios, not just equities.

corrections.issue: Speaker mostly wrong: Graham only says open source attracts the best technologists; the Arctic DB story and 'we open source a lot of the basic foundation' are Yav Git's (he was the initial sceptic at AHL).
corrections.fix: Graham Robertson and Yav Git: open-sourcing core infrastructure (e.g. Arctic DB) attracts top technologists and improved code quality at AHL; Yav says he was first sceptical and was proved wrong.

corrections.issue: Mixes speakers: the pressure on AHL's earnings from the liquid CTA program and the drive for Evolution diversity is Yav's point; Graham adds the range-bound markets and Fed put.
corrections.fix: Around 2011-2013 traditional liquid trend struggled in range-bound markets as the Fed put emerged (Graham); because AHL's earnings were tied to the liquid CTA program, this pushed it to diversify the Evolution program (Yav).
